I always wondered when someone was going to fill this niche.

Yeah. Given the differences between male and female bodies, it's also quite useful. As not many people cater to crossdressers or transgender people in the clothing department, this one could be fairly successful if he keeps it up, I think.

I think that he's not going into it thinking he's selling novelties will really help set him apart from any competition he might have, too. Where someone might make a line thinking only of making fetish wear, he's making things for real life, that you can really wear. I also liked this part:

Men would have to shop for very large sizes, which often ended up being pretty unflattering because the clothing was not designed for broad shoulders and the sleeves would come down too far on their wrists.

Large sizes fit no one correctly! I feel this so much. This is why I shop for my girl clothes in stores targeting bigger women. Normal department stores just blow up items that were designed for smaller women and it looks unflattering. We more rotund women need our clothing designed differently. (Incidentally, my boy clothes come from thrift stores, because that's where the best t-shirts are hiding. I live a double life of spending way too much and not enough. lol)

Yes. It would be good if there were something similar in the UK. I have a hard time finding appropriately sized clothing because, while as a male I'm unsuitable for smaller-sized female clothes, I'm thin for a male, so their larger sizes are often not the best fit either. I'll have to look into it and see if there is something of that type.

I suppose this is why so many people just learn to sew. Which is an idea!

I hope the transgender/cross dresser clothing thing picks up, I want to get the niche market for transgender/cross dresser targeted sewing patterns.

Ahh, I hadn't considered that. That would be useful, as a skill and as for crossdressing. How long does it take, roughly, to reach a point where you can make anything of decent use, though? Obviously it differs from person to person, but I mean in general.

Well, it really depends on what you start off making, how good your skills are with the machine, and how well you understand the construction of clothes. A lot of people just jump right in and start trying to make themselves stuff, but I find really grasping what goes into a piece to make it look the way it does instead of saying "It's a skirt, I know how this is done!" (happens more often than you'd think that a skirt is more complicated than just being a skirt) and charging in is more useful. Sewing has more planning than you might think, too.

But if you get down how the garment should be made, how it's going to hang on your body versus someone else's body, and all that, you'll be making decent clothes pretty quickly. It's less intimidating than it sounds, since once you figure out the basic way to make the style of a hemline, or a sleeve, and all that, you can pretty easily mix and match that skill with the dress, or shirt, or what have you to make something nice. Especially for cross dressing, you can learn to make a men's shirt, and just add the more feminine styles to that, and work with proportion. I would start with making purses and dolls, though. You need to get the machine skills on something you aren't going to get your hopes up for.

One interesting story unrelated to recent events is the corrupted blood incident. About ten years ago, World of Warcraft's latest content accidentally enabled players to infect others, killing low-level players and making npcs carriers. By ignorance or malice or curiosity, players brought this plague to high-traffic areas like the major cities, creating massive in-game casualties, to which the company hosting WoW tried to impose an in-game quarantine. People circumvented these efforts and the company had to go in to clean up the servers, applying quick fixes. Even though it was only a game, the mechanisms and reactions to this event have been studied by epidemiologists and commented on regarding terrorism. There's a wikipedia article on it, too.
